name: Forks
intro: A fork is one piece attacking two enemy pieces at once. Every piece can fork, even a pawn, but knights are famous for it: the forked pieces cannot block a knight's attack or hit back at it, unless one of them is a knight too. A fork that comes with check is the most powerful kind, because the king must move and the other piece is lost. Not every fork wins material, though: check how your opponent could escape before you play it.

parts.title: Check first, then the royal fork
parts.text: Soppe against Braga, Buenos Aires: you are Black. White's queen and king are both within a knight's jump of c3. Can you force them onto the right squares?

notes.text: The check leaves White one legal move: 41.Ke2. Now king on e2 and queen on d1 can both be hit from c3.
A royal fork: the knight checks the king and attacks the queen. The king must move, and the queen falls. In the game White resigned after 40...Qh1+.

parts.title: A fork that wins the exchange
parts.text: Tissir against Dreev, FIDE World Championship 2004: you are Black, and White's queen has just come to f4. Look for a knight check that leads to a fork.

notes.text: The knight checks from f2 and the king has to step to g1.
Now the knight attacks the queen on f4 and the rook on c1 at once. After the queen moves, Black takes the rook for a knight. White resigned here.

parts.title: The fork trick
parts.text: Two Knights Defence after 4.Nc3: you are Black. White has defended e4 with a knight, but a pawn fork lets you take it anyway.

notes.text: 4...Nxe4! seems to give a knight for a pawn, but it relies on the fork that follows.
After 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn attacks White's bishop and knight together. Whichever one moves, you win the other back and stand well in the centre.

name: Pins
intro: A pinned piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it. In an absolute pin the piece behind is the king, so moving the pinned piece is illegal. In a relative pin the piece behind is a queen or rook: the pinned piece may move, but it costs material. Once you have pinned a piece, look for a way to attack it again: it cannot run away.

parts.title: Attack the pinned piece
parts.text: Your bishop pins Black's rook on f7 to the king on g8. You could take the rook at once, but there is something stronger.

notes.text: Ng5! attacks the pinned rook a second time. It cannot move, and Black has no good way to defend it again, so Black will lose the rook. Taking on f7 at once only wins the exchange and leaves a close game. If you see a good move, look for a better one.

parts.title: A pin on the g-file
parts.text: A position from a game played on Lichess. White has just taken on g6. Find the pin that wins the bishop back.

parts.title: A pinned pawn
parts.text: A position from a game played on Lichess. Black has just attacked your knight with ...a6. Look at what is pinned on the e-file.

name: Skewers
intro: A skewer is a pin turned around. In a pin the less valuable piece stands in front of the more valuable one; in a skewer the more valuable piece is attacked first, and when it moves away the piece behind it is lost. Skewers through the king are the strongest, because the king must move.

parts.title: King in front of the queen
parts.text: Black's king has stepped onto d7, right in front of the queen on d8. How do you punish it?

notes.text: Either rook to d1 skewers king and queen. Black cannot block the check, so the king must move.
The king has moved out of the way and the queen behind it is lost.

parts.title: A queen skewer
parts.text: A position from a game played on Lichess. Black's king has just taken on c3. Find the check that wins Black's queen.

parts.title: A rook skewer
parts.text: A position from a game played on Lichess. White has just taken your bishop. Find the rook check that wins material back.

name: Discovered attacks
intro: A discovered attack happens when one piece moves out of the way and uncovers an attack by another piece behind it. Two pieces can then threaten at once. When the uncovered attack is a check it is a discovered check, and when the moving piece gives check as well it is a double check: the king must move, because two checks cannot both be blocked or captured.

parts.title: Discovered mate
parts.text: Your queen would be giving mate along the second rank, but your own pawn on d2 is in the way.

notes.text: The pawn steps aside and uncovers the queen's check. Black's king has no square left: discovered checkmate.

parts.title: Double check, then mate
parts.text: Your bishop on f4 aims at b8, but your knight on e5 blocks it. What happens when the knight moves with check?

notes.text: A double check: the knight checks from d7 and uncovers the bishop's check. The king has to move.
A sacrifice: the knight checks again and Black has to take it.
The pawn capture opens the a-file for your rook: another discovered check, and this time it is mate.

parts.title: A trap in the French
parts.text: French Defence, Advance Variation: Black has just grabbed a pawn with 8...Qxd4. Your bishop on d3 stands between your queen and Black's queen.

notes.text: The bishop moves with check and uncovers your queen's attack on d4. Black must deal with the check first.
Black's queen is lost: a whole queen won with one discovered attack.

name: Back-rank mate
intro: A back-rank mate is delivered by a rook or queen along the last rank, when the king cannot step forward because its own pawns block the way. The defending rook or queen that guards the back rank can often be lured away, exchanged or simply overloaded. To guard against it, give your king a flight square by moving one of the pawns in front of it.

parts.title: The bishop cannot be taken back
parts.line: Qxc6 Qa6 Qxa8 Rxa8 Rd8+ Rxd8 Rxd8#
parts.text: Your rooks are doubled on the d-file and Black's king has no flight square. Black's bishop on c6 is defended only by the rook on c8.

notes.text: Take the bishop. 1...Rxc6 would allow 2.Rd8+ Rxd8 3.Rxd8#, so Black is simply a piece down.
After 1...Qa6 the back rank is still weak: 2.Qxa8! takes a rook, and 2...Rxa8 would lose to mate.
The rook enters with check. Black can only block with the rook.
Mate on the back rank: the pawns on f7, g7 and h7 keep their own king in.

parts.title: Capablanca strikes
parts.line: Qb2 Qe1 Qxc3 Qxc3 Rd1+ Qe1 Rxe1#
parts.text: Bernstein against Capablanca, Moscow 1914: you are Black. White's queen guards the back rank and the rook on c3. Can you overload it?

notes.text: 29...Qb2! attacks the rook and offers the queen. 30.Qxb2 is impossible because of 30...Rd1#.
30.Qe1 seems to defend the rook, but the rook is not really protected: take it.
31.Qxc3 left the back rank, so the rook checks there. 32.Qe1 is the only block.
Back-rank mate.

parts.title: After the queen is gone
parts.text: A position from a game played on Lichess. White has just taken your queen on e4. White's king has no flight square: find the mate.

name: Removing the defender
intro: Removing the defender means capturing, chasing away or pinning the piece that guards something else, so that the piece it guarded is left hanging. Your opponent then has an unpleasant choice: take back, or save the piece that has lost its guard.

parts.title: Kramnik against Topalov
parts.text: Linares 2004: Black's knight on a4 is defended only by the pawn on b5.

notes.text: Take the defender. If 1...Rxb5, the knight on a4 is left alone; if 1...Nxb2, 2.Rb3 wins the exchange.
The knight falls, and White is a pawn up.

parts.title: Take the guard
parts.text: A position from a game played on Lichess. Black has just castled. Black's knight on e4 is attacked by your queen. What defends it?

parts.title: The rook that guards
parts.text: A position from a game played on Lichess. White has just offered a rook on d1 to your queen. Which white piece is doing two jobs?

name: Mate with king and queen
intro: Mating with king and queen against a lone king is easy once you know the method: use the queen alone to drive the enemy king to the edge of the board, keeping the queen a knight's move away from it, with no checks needed. Then bring your own king up to help, and watch out for stalemate. It takes about ten to fifteen moves.

parts.title: Drive the king to the edge
parts.line: Qb5 Ke6 Qc5 Kf6 Qd5 Kg6 Qe5 Kf7 Qd6 Kg7 Qe6 Kh7 Qg4 Kh6 Kb2
parts.text: First the queen works alone. Shrink the black king's space one rank or file at a time.

notes.text: Cut the black king off along the fifth rank.
Stay a knight's move away from the king. Checks like Qc6+ only give it more room.
The black king is now trapped on the edge, on the h-file.
Now that the king is stuck, your own king comes in to help finish the job.

parts.title: Finish the mate
parts.text: Your king has walked over to e5. Beware: Qg6 here would be stalemate, which is exactly what Black hopes for.

notes.text: Bring the king next to g7 so it can protect the queen there.
The queen, protected by the king, gives mate.

name: Mate with king and rook
intro: Mating with king and rook takes longer than with a queen, because king and rook must work together. The usual method is to build a box with the rook, protected by your own king, and make it smaller and smaller until the enemy king is pushed into a corner. No checks are needed until the final mate.

parts.title: Build the box
parts.line: Kc2 Ke5 Kd3 Kd5 Ra4 Ke5 Rd4 Kf5 Re4
parts.text: First improve your king, then use the rook to fence the black king into a box.

notes.text: Bring the king towards the centre before building the box.
The box is d8-d4-h4: the black king cannot cross the d-file or the fourth rank.
The box shrinks to e8-e4-h4.

parts.title: Creep closer
parts.line: Kf6 Kd4 Kf5 Kd5 Kf6 Re5
parts.text: The box is e8-e4-h4. Black's king is keeping its distance, so the rook cannot shrink the box straight away.

notes.text: The box can't be made smaller yet, so the king creeps closer.
Back to shrinking the box: the process repeats itself.

parts.title: Shrink the box to mate
parts.line: Ke5 Kf7 Kf5 Kg7 Rf6 Kh7 Rg6 Kh8 Kf6 Kh7 Kf7 Kh8 Rh6#
parts.text: After 8...Kf7 9.Re6 Kg7 the box is down to the last two ranks and files. Keep shrinking it with king and rook together; no checks are needed until the mate.

notes.text: The king follows the rook, keeping it protected.
Black's king can only shuffle between h7 and h8. If it were your move here, you would make a waiting move with the rook along the sixth rank.
Mate in the corner.

name: King and pawn endgames
intro: Two ideas decide most endgames with only kings and pawns: the rule of the square, which tells you whether a king can catch a pawn, and the opposition, the stand-off between two kings with one square between them. A passed pawn far from the other pawns, an outside passed pawn, is often enough to win.

parts.title: The rule of the square
parts.text: Draw a square from the pawn to its queening square (e5-e8-b8-b5). If the enemy king can step into it, it catches the pawn; if not, the pawn queens. Black's king on a4 is outside the square.

notes.text: With White to move the black king is outside the square, so just push.
The pawn queens. Had Black been to move, 1...Kb5 would have stepped into the square and caught it.

parts.title: The opposition
parts.line: Kd6 Kf5 Kd7 Kf6 Kd6 e4 Kd7 e5 Ke8 Ke6 Kd8 Kf7 Kd7 e6+ Kd6 e7
parts.text: The kings face each other with one square between them and it is Black to move, so you have the opposition: Black has to give way.

notes.text: Black's king stepped aside, so yours goes forward.
Black seems to have the opposition now, but you don't have to move your king: a pawn move hands the move back to Black.
Your king stands in front of the pawn on the sixth rank, and the pawn will get through.
The pawn queens next move.

parts.title: The outside passed pawn
parts.line: f5 Kd6 f6 Ke6 Kxc5 Kxf6 Kb6 Ke6 Kxa6 Kd7 Kb7
parts.text: Pawns are equal, but your f-pawn is far from the others. Use it as a decoy.

notes.text: Push the outside pawn so the black king has to chase it.
While Black's king is away, yours eats the queenside pawns.
Your king shields the a-pawn, and it will queen.

name: Rook endgames: Lucena and Philidor
intro: Rook and pawn against rook is the most common endgame of all, and two positions are the key to it. With the Lucena position the side with the pawn wins by building a bridge with the rook to shelter its king. With the Philidor position the defender draws by keeping the rook on the third rank and then checking from behind.

parts.title: Lucena: build a bridge
parts.line: Rd1+ Ke7 Rd4 Ra1 Kc7 Rc1+ Kb6 Rb1+ Kc6 Rc1+ Kb5 Rb1+ Rb4
parts.text: Your pawn is on the seventh rank but your own king stands in front of it, and Black's rook is ready to check.

notes.text: Drive the black king away from the pawn first.
The key move: the rook goes to the fourth rank, ready to block checks later.
Now the king comes out, and Black starts checking.
The rook blocks the check: the bridge is built. Black cannot stop the pawn queening.

parts.title: Philidor: hold the draw
parts.line: Rb2 Rc3 Ra2 Rb3 e3 Rb8 Kf3 Rf8+ Ke4 Re8+ Kf4 Rf8+ Ke5 Re8+
parts.text: You defend. Your king is on the pawn's queening square and your rook on the third rank keeps Black's king out.

notes.text: Keep the rook on the third rank, shuffling along it, until the pawn comes forward.
With the pawn on e3, Black's king can no longer use that square, so your rook is free to go to the far end of the board. 4.Rb4+?? would lose to 4...Kf3.
Check from behind. The king cannot escape the checks without giving up the pawn.
Black makes no progress: a draw.
